definition: Overly dramatic or emotional in a way that seems meant to draw attention.
example: His histrionic sighs over slightly cold soup made everyone at the dinner table roll their eyes.
nuance: Unlike genuine distress, histrionic behavior implies the feelings are inflated or performed for an audience.
prompt: A student reacts to getting a B-plus on a short quiz.
options: Her histrionic wail over a B-plus made the whole row of students turn around.
The histrionic quiz was preserved in the school archive as an important record.
Her histrionic response was a small shrug before she slipped the quiz into her bag.
Her histrionic grasp of fractions explained why she missed only one problem.
reasons: A loud, exaggerated outburst over a good grade is a showy display out of proportion to the event.
This confuses the word with historic; a quiz cannot put on an exaggerated emotional show.
A quiet shrug is understated, the opposite of an overblown performance.
The word describes overdone emotional display, not skill or understanding.

practice.prompt: An office worker finds that someone left the coffee pot empty.
options: The histrionic coffee pot had sat on the same counter since the office first opened.
His histrionic reaction was to rinse the pot without a word and brew a fresh one.
Being histrionic, he measured the coffee grounds to the exact gram every morning.
His histrionic groan about the empty pot echoed down the hallway for a minute.
reasons: Being old or long-standing relates to history, not to exaggerated emotion.
Fixing the problem silently shows calm restraint, not dramatic excess.
Precise measuring reflects carefulness, which has nothing to do with theatrical behavior.
A long, loud groan over a minor annoyance is theatrical and attention-seeking.
